To prove that the functors $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-, -)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-, -) \circ (L^{\text{op}} \times \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C})$ are equal, we must demonstrate that they have the same domain and codomain, and that they agree on all objects and all morphisms.

Both functors have domain $\mathbf D^{\text{op}} \times \mathbf C$ and codomain $\mathbf{Set}$.

**Equality on Objects:**
Let $(D, C)$ be an arbitrary object in $\mathbf D^{\text{op}} \times \mathbf C$, where $D \in \operatorname{ob}(\mathbf D^{\text{op}}) = \operatorname{ob}(\mathbf D)$ and $C \in \operatorname{ob}(\mathbf C)$. 
By the definition of the hom bifunctor with a left functor, its action on objects is given by:
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-, -)(D, C) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD, C)$$

For the right-hand side, evaluating the composite functor on $(D, C)$ gives:
$$(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-, -) \circ (L^{\text{op}} \times \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}))(D, C) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-, -)(L^{\text{op}}(D), \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}(C))$$
By the definition of the opposite functor, $L^{\text{op}}(D) = LD$, and by the definition of the identity functor, $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}(C) = C$. Substituting these yields:
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-, -)(LD, C) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD, C)$$
Thus, both functors yield the identical set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD, C)$, confirming they agree on all objects.

**Equality on Morphisms:**
Let $(f^{\text{op}}, g) : (D_1, C_1) \to (D_2, C_2)$ be an arbitrary morphism in $\mathbf D^{\text{op}} \times \mathbf C$. 
Here, $f^{\text{op}} : D_1 \to D_2$ is a morphism in $\mathbf D^{\text{op}}$, which corresponds to a morphism $f : D_2 \to D_1$ in $\mathbf D$. Meanwhile, $g : C_1 \to C_2$ is a morphism in $\mathbf C$.

Applying the left-hand side functor to $(f^{\text{op}}, g)$ gives a mapping between hom-sets:
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(L-, -)(f^{\text{op}}, g) : \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD_1, C_1) \to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD_2, C_2)$$
By definition, for any element $h \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD_1, C_1)$ (which is a morphism $h : LD_1 \to C_1$ in $\mathbf C$), this functor maps $h$ to the composition:
$$g \circ h \circ L(f)$$
(Note that since $f : D_2 \to D_1$ in $\mathbf D$, we have $L(f) : LD_2 \to LD_1$ in $\mathbf C$. The composition $LD_2 \xrightarrow{L(f)} LD_1 \xrightarrow{h} C_1 \xrightarrow{g} C_2$ is well-defined and yields a valid morphism in $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD_2, C_2)$.)

For the right-hand side, we evaluate the composite functor on the morphism $(f^{\text{op}}, g)$:
$$(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-, -) \circ (L^{\text{op}} \times \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}))(f^{\text{op}}, g) = \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-, -)(L^{\text{op}}(f^{\text{op}}), \operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}(g))$$
By the definition of the opposite functor $L^{\text{op}}$, its action on a morphism $f^{\text{op}}$ is $(L(f))^{\text{op}}$, which is a morphism $LD_1 \to LD_2$ in $\mathbf C^{\text{op}}$. 
Additionally, $\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf C}(g) = g$. Thus, we are evaluating the standard hom bifunctor $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-, -)$ on the pair $((L(f))^{\text{op}}, g)$.
The standard hom bifunctor $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(-, -) : \mathbf C^{\text{op}} \times \mathbf C \to \mathbf{Set}$ acts on a morphism pair $(\phi^{\text{op}}, \psi)$ by mapping any $h$ in its domain to $\psi \circ h \circ \phi$. 
Substituting $\phi = L(f)$ and $\psi = g$, the functor maps any $h \in \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf C}(LD_1, C_1)$ to:
$$g \circ h \circ L(f)$$

Both the left-hand side functor and the right-hand side composite functor map an arbitrary morphism $(f^{\text{op}}, g)$ to exactly the same function $h \mapsto g \circ h \circ L(f)$. Therefore, they agree on all morphisms.

Since the two functors have the same domain and codomain, and agree on all objects and morphisms, they are identical. This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$
